newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan lets foreigners trade in debt instruments.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan lets foreigners trade in debt instruments.

text.p: Pakistan stands to attract millions of dollars in foreign exchange after the central bank allowed non-resident investors to trade freely in private and public debt instruments, analysts said on Tuesday.
Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz told reporters in Islamabad that foreign investment in government securities and corporate fixed-income securities would be made tax-free.
Analysts said a circular issued by the State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP) and Aziz's statement effectively removed all restrictions on bond trading by foreign investors.
The removal of taxation was even more important and would eventually lead to higher foreign investment in fixed-income instruments, the analysts said.

"We will have to wait for a notice from the CBR (Central Board of Revenue)...to see what the actual tax liability will now be for different categories of foreign investors," forex analyst Faheem Ahmed of Banque Indo Suez told Reuters.

Analysts said foreign institutions and banks previously had to pay up to 60 percent and individuals 32.5 percent in non-refundable withholding tax and an additional 2.5 percent as Zakat (Islamic tax) on earnings from debt instruments.

"The high withholding tax was the single major deterrent that discouraged foreign investors from investing in rupee-based debt instruments," Anisur Rehman, research head at SocGen Crosby Securities, said.

He said if the tax was scrapped or cut to the level payable by local investors, who pay only 10 percent withholding tax and 2.5 percent Zakat, foreigners would be more than willing to invest in government and private corporate debt issues.
Rehman said annual yields for most Pakistani debt issues were in the 16.50 to 19 percent range, well above average yields in most other countries in the region.
Senior analyst Arshad Arif of ING Baring Securities said opening up the bond market would help the government attract foreign currency and boost the corporate debt market.
Raza Mirza, research head at KASB & Co, said the government had been contemplating the move for some time.
"As there was little or no investment in government debt instruments, the government was getting nothing in taxes anyway," he said.
By removing the tax on fixed-income securities, the government would lure investment which could boost its foreign exchange reserves and ease its foreign debt repayment problems.
Pakistan's cash reserves stood at $882 million on April 26, down from $910 million a week earlier. Analysts say it faces debt repayments of more than $1.5 billion in July-September.

The SBP circular said foreign investors, including overseas Pakistanis, would be allowed to invest in bonds and term finance certificates, including federal investment bonds and treasury bills, listed in Pakistani stock exchanges in the secondary market through special convertible rupee accounts.
